subsystems.name: Beam and field sources
subsystems.role: the only tools known to reach individual nuclei: high-energy particles, photons and confining fields.

subsystems.name: Nucleon-rearrangement stage
subsystems.role: would excite, compress or collide nuclei so their protons and neutrons regroup into new configurations.

subsystems.name: Metastable-state store
subsystems.role: would hold a rearranged nucleus alive long enough to build with it — excitement energy stored in nuclear isomers.

subsystems.name: Containment and assembly cell
subsystems.role: would stop the product from flying apart; nuclei at nuclear density repel nothing electrically at close range, but the energies involved are millions of times chemical ones.

subsystems.name: Energy and waste handling
subsystems.role: every rearrangement releases or absorbs MeV-scale energy, mostly as gamma rays, neutrons and heat.

buildSteps.title: Isolate the feedstock
buildSteps.detail: Choose and separate specific isotopes, then ionise them — ordinary nuclear physics, done routinely at accelerators.

buildSteps.title: Inject energy at nuclear scale
buildSteps.detail: Fire beams or intense gamma rays at the nuclei. This costs MeV per nucleus, millions of times more than a chemical reaction, so the energy bill dominates everything.

buildSteps.title: Force the rearrangement
buildSteps.detail: In known physics this step is a collision or excitation, not a directed assembly. Products come out as a statistical mix, so selectivity would have to be engineered, not assumed.

buildSteps.title: Catch and stabilise the product
buildSteps.detail: Most nuclei formed this way are unstable and decay in seconds or less; a practical route would need to land on or near the 'island of stability' (a region of superheavy nuclei predicted by nuclear theory but never confirmed).

buildSteps.title: Cool and shield the product
buildSteps.detail: Absorb the burst of gamma rays and neutrons and extract the remaining heat — otherwise the material destroys its own container.

buildSteps.title: Assemble bulk matter
buildSteps.detail: The core obstacle: matter at nuclear density, about 10^17 kg per cubic metre, is only known to exist inside neutron stars, where gravity supplies the confining pressure. No lab-scale way to hold such material together has ever been proposed in workable detail.

buildSteps.title: Account for the energy balance
buildSteps.detail: Compare the energy spent rearranging nuclei with what the material could usefully store or release. Whether any configuration is a net energy win is unknown.

prerequisites.why: today's accelerators produce statistical sprays of products, not engineered single nuclei.
driving nuclear transitions efficiently needs coherent high-energy photons; no such source has ever been built, and mirrors for gamma rays barely exist.
nuclear physics and neutron-star observations give equations of state for bulk nuclear matter, but not engineering-grade control at small scale.
nuclear isomers that store energy in excited states are real, and triggering them has been studied for decades without a demonstrated practical control method.
MeV-per-nucleus processing, if it could be done at all, would need an energy plant many orders of magnitude beyond any built.

pathway.milestone: heavy-ion colliders briefly create quark-gluon plasma, and accelerator labs transmute nuclei one collision at a time
pathway.unlocks: data on nuclear structure and on matter far from everyday conditions — not yet building blocks.

pathway.milestone: better models of nuclear excited states and confirmed predictions in the island of stability
pathway.unlocks: knowing whether stable superheavy configurations exist to build from.
the first conceivable tool for acting on individual nuclei rather than smashing them.

pathway.milestone: controlled rearrangement of a single nucleus with a chosen outcome
pathway.unlocks: microscopic quantities of engineered nuclear matter — if it is physically possible at all.

pathway.milestone: a way to hold nuclear-density matter together without gravity
pathway.unlocks: bulk materials at nuclear density would overturn what is currently known about stable matter; failing that, this remains theory.
